messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Vignette:
John is a 67-year-old widowed man with Oceania heritage who works as an interior designer. His life took a profound turn following his captivity experience several years ago in which he was held hostage and subjected to intense psychological trauma. The vivid memories of that event have deeply impacted John's daily functioning, leading him to seek help due to the overwhelming burden of his symptoms. The traumatic event occurred during a business trip to the Middle East where John was taken captive by a group who demanded ransom from his family. During this period, he was subjected to verbal and emotional abuse, with constant shouting in Arabic that deeply disturbed him. These auditory triggers now emerge spontaneously, often causing intense distress when he hears similar sounds. John's memory of the event is fragmented and emotionless. He can recall details but feels completely detached, as if recounting someone else’s experience. When he tries to share his story, he frequently loses track of what he wants to say and cannot finish explaining it coherently. These memories are further complicated by auditory intrusions; John often hears voices in his head repeating the harsh commands and threats from his captors. Since the event, John has become hyper-vigilant and avoids enclosed spaces where he feels trapped or confined. His daily routine as an interior designer has been significantly impacted by this avoidance behavior. He now finds it difficult to work on projects that require him to be in small, closed rooms, leading to delays and frustration at work. To cope with his anxiety, John rehearses what he will say before any social interaction, a maladaptive strategy that stems from his fear of not being able to respond adequately. John's sense of vulnerability is heightened by the feeling that he cannot protect himself or predict when danger might arise again. He harbors a strong belief that his body reacts to perceived threats even before his mind can process them. This intense emotional response includes feelings of fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame, which often leave him feeling overwhelmed. John has come to believe that safety lies in having his back against a wall where he can see everything around him. This belief has influenced many aspects of his life. He rearranges furniture at home so that he is always positioned with his back to a wall when sitting or standing. At work, he avoids client meetings in enclosed spaces and often insists on holding them in open areas. The cumulative effect of these avoidance behaviors has strained John’s relationships and professional life. His colleagues have noticed changes in his demeanor and work habits, leading to misunderstandings and diminished trust. The strain is particularly evident during interactions where his rehearsed conversations feel forced and unnatural. What frightened John most was the realization that despite his efforts to control every situation, he remained acutely aware of his vulnerability. He feared that another traumatic event could occur at any moment, leaving him helpless once again. These fears had grown so intense that they were affecting his daily life in profound ways, leading him to seek help. John is most hoping for a sense of safety and stability. He wants to regain control over his thoughts and emotions without having to constantly monitor his surroundings or rehearse every interaction. Through therapy, he hopes to find ways to process the traumatic memories and reduce their impact on his life, ultimately finding peace in his daily existence again.
